newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Lion sets sights on Australia, China.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Lion sets sights on Australia, China.

text.p: Lion Nathan Ltd said on Thursday the year to August had been difficult, but it saw potential in the Australian premium beer market and in greater involvement in China, where it already has a presence.

Lion Chief Executive Douglas Myers told a news conference that while the company would continue its focus on crunching costs, it saw opportunities across the Tasman where it considered the premium sector to be underdeveloped.
"The development of the premium beer market has been one of the factors which has enabled us to grow our profits in New Zealand and the same opportunity exists in Australia," Myers said.
"We have plans for the premium segment in Australia, so watch this space," he said, without elaborating.
New Zealand premium beers represented 11 percent of the total domestic market, and growth in this sector was accelerating.
Myers said he expected premium beers to form 20 percent of the local market by 2000. By contrast, the sector represented just two percent of the market at present.
The company earlier reported a net profit after tax of NZ$150.4 million (US$106.24 million), down from $202.3 million a year earlier, due to an increase in the tax charge of NZ$76 million.
Myers said that had been a challenging year, the company increased earnings from operations, made progress in China and further strengthened its cash flow.
With the marketing structure now complete in Australia, he was confident the company could lift its performance there.
Australia, which represents about two thirds of Lion's operations, had a tough year, with earnings and market share down slightly.
Against this background, there was declining overall beer consumption in both countries.

Lion continued its love affair with China, where it has a controlling interest in a brewery at Wuxi, in the Yangtse Delta, and one under construction at Souzhou, by announcing it planned to buy another plant in the area within 12-18 months.
Myers said the new China brewery would be similar in size to its Wuxi plant.

"We continue to review opportunities for new investment in other existing breweries within the Yangtse delta region, consistent with our strategy of achieving a critical mass of volume within a prosperous area," he said.
Myers said the company had cooled its ambitions for India, preferring instead to become "more engrossed" with China.

Lion's balance sheet continued to strengthen, with gearing down to 69 percent after repaying NZ$650 million in debt over the last four years, and raising the likelihood of a ratings upgrade in the years to come.
Standard and Poor's currently rates the company's longterm debt at BB plus.
Analysts' reaction to the result was mixed, with John Cairns at Cavill White Securities describing it as "ordinary".
But the share market approved, taking the stock up eight cents to close at NZ$3.65.
